job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Carla Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now, in your job hunt, your first job or your studies.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior design technician at a family-owned firm in Derby that makes industrial pumps. I studied mechanical engineering, passed with an average mark and did no placement, and I've been there six months. I draw parts in CAD, which is design software, then walk down to the workshop to check them against the real thing. I love the workshop, the smell of cutting oil and the old fitters who tell me everything I drew wrong. I rent a room in a house with four others, and my room costs more than I think it should. I've never used an AI tool and I don't plan to, because I prefer to know how I got an answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's about what I thought. At work I'd say nothing, because it's what the owner Mr Barlow says too, that computers come and go. To my friends I'd say I'm glad, because I'd like to keep what I've learned. Online I'd say no comment, I don't do online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means my life stays exactly as stretched as it is. The firm's busy and fairly stable, so I'm not afraid for my job, but my wage is low, my loan is large, and the rent keeps going up. I keep an eye on how much I've got saved, which is less than one month. That's what I worry about, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd do overtime when it's offered, put a bit away each month, and keep learning the machines in the workshop from the fitters. I'd look at whether I can pay my loan a different way. And I'd stay in my room, because moving costs a deposit I don't have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels calm on the AI side and tense on the money side. So, a mixture. I'd say mostly steady, with a stone in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the overtime change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About £180 extra a month, if I get four Saturdays. That would go straight on the loan or into the savings account. The fitters work Saturdays anyway, and I'd rather be there than in my room. It's tiring, but at least I'm learning something while I earn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've never used an AI tool. Is there anything that would make you try one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Mr Barlow told me to, I'd try it. But I wouldn't go looking. I don't like not knowing why a thing gives me an answer. In my job a wrong dimension means a wrong part, and a wrong part costs money. So I'd need to see it right a hundred times before I trusted it.

say: I'd say it's about what I **expected** and I'm glad to keep what I've learned.
At work I'd say **nothing**, like the owner Mr Barlow.
think: My life stays **stretched**: low wage, large loan, rising rent.
I'm not afraid for my job, but less than one month **saved** worries me.
do: Take Saturday **overtime** for about £180 a month towards the loan.
Keep learning the **machines** in the workshop from the fitters.
Stay in my rented **room**, since moving needs a deposit.
feel: Calm about AI and tense about **money**, like a stone in my stomach.
S0.quote: In my job a wrong dimension means a wrong part, and a wrong part costs money.
fieldNote: She **separates** AI from money worry cleanly, which shows how little AI touches her day.
Her reluctance is about knowing why an answer is right, not fear.
Overtime is the realistic lever she has.

steps.text: Take four Saturday overtime shifts a month in the workshop
Keep learning the machines from the fitters

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming whether I like it or not. At work I'd tell Mr Barlow that the drawing team has to be careful what we hand over to software. To friends I'd say it'll change the office jobs first, and I hope it doesn't change the workshop. Online I'd say nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, a lot of my work is drawing and checking dimensions, and I know that's the sort of thing the software now does. Mr Barlow went to a trade show and came back full of ideas. I think there'll be fewer of us in the design office in three years, and I'm the newest. What I do in the workshop is the part nobody's trying to automate yet, so that's where I'd want to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to spend more of my week in the workshop, doing fit and test work. I'd take a night class on welding or machining, to be useful on the floor. I'd keep my spending very low. And I'd still avoid the AI software for a while, though if Mr Barlow insists I'd learn what I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the ground is moving slowly under me. Not a crash, but I can't pretend I don't feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the design office would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gordon, the senior draughtsman, who's sixty-one and draws everything by hand first. He'll be offered early retirement, I think, and he doesn't want it. He's taught me half of what I know. If the firm cuts, they'll cut the oldest or the newest, and I'd be a bit ashamed if it was my colleague Gordon and not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you ask Mr Barlow to move you to the workshop without sounding like you're scared?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I want to understand how the parts behave after they're made, so my drawings get better. That's true. He likes people who say that. I wouldn't say I'm afraid for my job, because it would sound like I was complaining.

say: I'd tell the owner Mr Barlow to be careful what the design team hands to **software**.
I'd hope AI changes office jobs but not the **workshop**.
think: Drawing and checking dimensions is the sort of work **software** does now.
There'll be fewer in the design office in three years, and I'm the **newest**.
do: Ask to spend more of my week in the **workshop** on fit and test work.
Take a night class in **welding** or machining.
feel: The ground moving slowly, not a crash, but I can't **pretend** I don't feel it.
S1.quote: If the firm cuts, they'll cut the oldest or the newest, and I'd be a bit ashamed if it was my colleague Gordon and not me.
fieldNote: She chooses the **workshop** as her protection, which fits her resistance to screen tools.
Guilt about older colleague Gordon shows loyalty over self-interest.
She wouldn't admit fear to the owner, a gap between private and public.

steps.text: Ask Mr Barlow to put me on workshop fit and test work
Enrol in an evening machining course at the college
Cut my food and transport budget by £50 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is crazy and nobody's ready, including the firm. At work I'd say we need a plan for the people who draw, and I'd say it to Mr Barlow's face if he asked. To friends I'd say get your money safe and learn something you can do with your hands. Online I'd say nothing, but I'd vote for whoever promised help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means my degree is worth little by 2028. Everything I was trained to do on a screen, the machine does better. I'd be lucky to hold on until robots reach the workshop, around 2031. That's a gap of three years and I'd need to live through it on very little. I'm scared, quite honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the design office as soon as the workshop would take me, even in a lower-paid job, because it lasts longer. I'd move back to my dad's flat in Burton for a year if I had to, which he'd welcome. I'd stop anything that isn't rent and food. And I'd start a machining apprenticeship, because my hands are the part of me that robots take last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a door slamming. I'm numb and a bit furious, because I did the sensible thing, got the degree, got the job and still lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move back to your dad's. How does he feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's a retired bus driver and he's got a one-bedroom flat with a sofa bed. He'd say yes straight away, and he'd cook me tea every night, which would make it worse for my pride. I'd pay him what I could. I'd tell him it's only for a year, and we'd both know it might not be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When you say you did the sensible thing, who do you blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not Mr Barlow, he's been fair. I blame the people who said get a degree and you'll be fine, and the companies who built this knowing what it would do. And I blame the government a bit for not warning us. I wouldn't scream at anyone, I'd just feel cheated.

say: I'd say two years is **crazy**, nobody's ready, and the firm needs a plan for people who draw.
I'd tell friends to get their money **safe** and learn something with their hands.
think: My degree is worth little by 2028, and I'd need to **survive** three years before robots reach the workshop.
do: Leave the design office for the **workshop**, even at lower pay.
Move back to my dad's **flat** in Burton for a year.
feel: A door **slamming**, numb and furious that I did the sensible thing and still lose.
S2.quote: I did the sensible thing, got the degree, got the job and still lose.
fieldNote: She sees the **3-year** robot gap as the thing she has to bridge, with her dad's sofa bed as the bridge.
Blame falls on those who sold the degree, not on her firm.
Pride matters more than the move itself.

steps.text: Ask to move from the design office to the workshop
Move into my dad's flat in Burton for a year
Cut spending to rent and food only

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough that people will have to make a decision and short enough that you can't dither. At work I'd say let's train people up for the workshop side. To friends I'd say plan, don't panic. Online, no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think it's manageable if I start acting by next year. My plan is to be good with my hands and good at the design side, so I'm useful in both. I'd like to be the person who can walk from the drawing to the machine and tell them what's wrong. That person lasts longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the evening machining course this winter, about £600, paid in instalments. I'd save £80 a month towards a six-week cushion. I'd ask Mr Barlow for a training day each month in the workshop. And I'd still avoid AI tools, but I'd learn the one the firm buys, because I'd have no choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels better than I'd expected. There's a sense of having time, which counts for a lot. I'm still a bit tense about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the firm's tool because you'd have no choice. What would that be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like learning a new lathe. Slowly, with my arms folded. But once I know what it does, I'm fine. I just don't like pretending something's good when I haven't checked. The fitters would have the same attitude, so I'd feel less alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a six-week cushion mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I could get through a gap between jobs without calling my dad. It's about £2,400 at my rent. I'd feel much safer. It would take me about thirty months at £80, so I'd need a bit of luck, like a pay rise.

say: I'd say five years is enough to decide but too **short** to dither.
I'd tell friends to **plan**, not panic.
think: It's **manageable** if I act by next year and stay useful at both design and workshop.
The person who can walk from the drawing to the **machine** lasts longer.
do: Take the evening **machining** course this winter, about £600 in instalments.
Save **£80** a month towards a six-week cushion.
Ask Mr Barlow for a monthly **training day** in the workshop.
feel: Better than I'd expected, with a sense of having **time**.
S3.quote: I just don't like pretending something's good when I haven't checked.
fieldNote: Her **resistance** shows as a need to test things, not as denial.
She sets a figure for her cushion and admits it takes thirty months.
Time lowers fear but money keeps her anxious.

steps.text: Enrol in the £600 evening machining course this winter
Save £80 a month towards a £2,400 cushion
Ask Mr Barlow for a monthly training day in the workshop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and plenty of things will change before then. At work I'd say let's keep training people. To friends I'd say not to worry too much yet. Online I'd say nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I don't feel it threatens me much. In ten years I could be a design engineer with some seniority, or a workshop supervisor. I'd have paid down some of the loan. I think the firm will still be here, because people will still want pumps. That doesn't mean I'm not worried about the other things, like rent and prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and do the evening course. I'd save up for a deposit on a small place, if prices allow. I'd look at part-time study towards chartered engineer status. And I'd still not use AI unless I had to, but I'd keep my ears open for what the older fitters say about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels fine, honestly. I'd say calm, but with the same stone about money that never quite goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'plenty of things will change.' What do you worry about that I haven't asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent and prices. My room's gone up twice in a year and my pay hasn't. If the world runs on AI and the rich get richer, I'm afraid everyday costs won't come down for people like me. It's the boring stuff that gets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a graduate starting next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn something you can do with your hands, as well as on a screen. Find the older people in the firm who know why things are done a certain way, and listen. And try to save from your first pay cheque, even a little, because it's the first year that hurts most.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long time** and plenty will change before then.
I'd tell friends **not** to worry too much yet.
think: I don't feel it threatens me much, and the firm will still make **pumps**.
I still worry about **rent** and prices rather than AI.
do: Do the evening **machining** course and carry on at the firm.
Save for a **deposit** on a small place if prices allow.
feel: Fine, nearly calm, with the same **stone** about money that never quite goes.
S4.quote: My room's gone up twice in a year and my pay hasn't.
fieldNote: Her calm is **real** but sits next to everyday cost worries.
She gives sensible advice to a future graduate and puts saving first.
The one step she keeps resisting is AI.

steps.text: Finish the evening machining course and keep the firm job
Save for a flat deposit from the first pay cheque each month
Start part-time study towards chartered engineer status

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. The drawing work goes first, and I'd have no savings and a loan. What would help is a decent government plan for people like me, and firms keeping a few trainees on to learn the hands-on side. And a rent I can live on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people say my generation is soft or too online. I'm not either. I like a workshop and a straight answer. If someone gave me a proper apprenticeship and a fair wage, I'd work harder than most. I'd like someone to notice that.

headlineQuote: If someone gave me a proper apprenticeship and a fair wage, I'd work harder than most.
portrait: Carla is a 22-year-old mechanical engineering graduate working as a **junior design technician** at a family pump firm in Derby.
She is centrist and resistant: she has never used AI and likes to know why an answer is right.
She rents a room, owes a large loan and has under a month saved, so **money** worries run through everything.
She trusts the workshop and its older fitters, and plans her future around hands-on skills.
Two years alarms her, while ten years leaves her nearly calm.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because screen-based design goes first and she would have no savings.
whatWouldHelp: A real government **plan**, firms keeping trainees for hands-on work, and rent she can live on.
